analysis.one_liner: Taxes drug companies 10% of income unless they charge Americans their lowest foreign prices.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Sen. Carl Levin in September 2000, never left the Senate Finance Committee and never got a vote before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have put a 10% tax on the income of any prescription drug manufacturer unless, with its tax return, a senior officer signed a statement — under penalty of perjury — that the company does not charge US wholesale distributors more for bulk purchases than the best price it gives wholesalers in Canada or any European Union country. Money raised by the tax would go to the Medicare hospital insurance trust fund. Companies could avoid the tax simply by ending the practice of charging Americans more than foreign customers.
analysis.who_benefits: American patients, insurers, and government programs that pay US prescription drug prices. The bill's leverage is aimed at the gap that lets drug makers charge US wholesalers more than they charge Canadian and European wholesalers for the same bulk purchases. If companies complied rather than pay the tax, Americans would get the same best price foreigners already receive; if they did not comply, the 10% income tax revenue would flow to Medicare's hospital insurance trust fund.

how_it_helps.text: The bill imposes a 10% tax on a drug maker's taxable income if the company fails to file a signed statement, under penalty of perjury by a senior officer, that it does not charge US wholesalers a higher bulk-purchase price than its best price to wholesalers in Canada or European Union countries.

The 'most favored customer price' is defined as the best unit price available to any wholesale distributor for comparable bulk purchases, so US buyers could not be charged more than the company's most favored foreign customers.
Revenue from the new tax would be dedicated to the Federal Hospital Insurance Trust Fund, which funds Medicare's hospital coverage.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, either by giving up the higher prices they charge US wholesalers (their main source of above-foreign pricing) or by paying a tax equal to 10% of their entire taxable income — a far heavier penalty than the pricing gap itself, designed to make compliance the cheaper option.

drawbacks.text: Enforcement rests on companies policing themselves: the bill collects no pricing data itself and instead relies on a chief financial officer's signed statement under penalty of perjury, so the Internal Revenue Service would have to audit and litigate pricing claims across dozens of foreign markets.

The strongest good-faith objection is that compressing US prices toward lower foreign levels reduces revenue that funds pharmaceutical research and development, which manufacturers argue would slow the development of new drugs.

A compliance tax of 10% of all taxable income is an all-or-nothing penalty triggered by a single nonconforming bulk sale, which could push companies toward uniform pricing abroad or pulling products from smaller foreign markets rather than lowering US prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real, well-known gap: the same drug often costs more per unit in the US than in Canada or Europe. Its design is blunt but pointed — a company either matches its best foreign price for Americans or pays a tax far larger than the pricing gap, with proceeds going to Medicare. The honest costs are enforcement through self-certification rather than direct price regulation, the risk that companies adjust foreign markets instead of US prices, and the drug industry's argument that lower returns mean less research spending. On balance, the direct benefit to US drug purchasers is large and the compliance burden falls on the companies profiting from the price gap.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late September 2000, read twice, and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up; the Congress ended in early January 2001, so the bill died in committee.

narrative.text: Sen. Carl Levin (D-MI) introduced S. 3103 on September 25, 2000, joined by one cosponsor, Sen. Richard Bryan (D-NV).
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day; no further action was recorded before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.
It was introduced in the final weeks of a congressional session, when the Senate Finance Committee had little remaining time to act on new tax legislation.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies kept the freedom to charge US wholesale distributors more than Canadian and European buyers, and the Medicare trust fund never received the new tax revenue.

for.name: Sen. Carl Levin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Michigan; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral for tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 25, 2000 and took no action on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only two senators, both Democrats, put their names on the bill, and it never came to a vote, so no party split was ever tested; its referral to the tax-writing Finance Committee was the end of the road.

industries.note: The bill would force them to charge US wholesalers no more than their best Canadian and European bulk prices or pay a tax equal to 10% of their taxable income. It attacks the practice of charging Americans the highest prices in the developed world, so the industry's gain from the bill's failure is Americans' continued cost.

industries.industry: US pharmacy and drug retail sector
industries.note: Pharmacies and retailers buy from US wholesalers, so lower wholesale prices would reduce their acquisition costs and could be passed to consumers. The bill does not directly regulate them.
